St. Tikhon of Zadonsk

St. Tikhon of Zadonsk

St. Tikhon Sokolov · St. Tikhon Sokolovsky

Period
1724–1783
Region
Russia
Titles / vocation
Hierarch · Monastic
Commemoration

Introduction

St. Tikhon of Zadonsk is the Russian bishop and author, distinct from Patriarch St. Tikhon of Moscow.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Repose following illness, August 13, 1783.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The official life describes a poor childhood, education at Novgorod, and teaching before monastic tonsure and episcopal service.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 3; Published biographical account,paragraph 4; Published biographical account,paragraph 5

Life and notable events

As bishop of Voronezh he works for clergy formation and pastoral order. Ill health leads to retirement, and the life describes charity and writing at Zadonsk.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 6; Published biographical account,paragraph 14; Published biographical account,paragraph 17

Elena Sapaeva’s account begins with poverty and the death of Tikhon’s father. It describes the older brother’s support for schooling and the young man’s progress to teaching. The account then follows the large Voronezh diocese and deteriorating health that brought retirement. Its descriptions of his emotional distress belong to this published biographical portrayal; the app is not diagnosing a historical person or prescribing treatment.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 5; Published biographical account,paragraph 6; Published biographical account,paragraph 9; Published biographical account,paragraph 14; Published biographical account,paragraph 16

The official life presents education as a sustained concern: he taught before episcopal consecration and later addressed the formation of clergy. Its retirement account describes help to people in need and deliberate simplicity in personal life. The later honor of his relics is distinguished from his lifetime service, and the 1846 uncovering is not confused with the 1861 glorification.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 29; Published biographical account,paragraph 30

Death and martyrdom

The source records repose on August 13, 1783, at 59, and later uncovering of relics and glorification. It does not report martyrdom.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 15; Published biographical account,paragraph 30

Writings and legacy

His books and pastoral correspondence are central to his reception. The separately authored account below discusses his difficult retirement and care for visitors.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 6; Published biographical account,paragraph 17 · [2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 9; Published biographical account,paragraph 16

The article describes the books A Spiritual Treasure Collected From the World and On True Christianity, and continuing correspondence. It portrays a retirement devoted to visitors, material help, and care for the sick rather than inactivity. Near the end, it recounts increasing weakness, reclusion, and letters to spiritual children before repose. These details supplement the official life while remaining the account’s own historical and devotional framing.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 9; Published biographical account,paragraph 13; Published biographical account,paragraph 14; Published biographical account,paragraph 16

Archbishop Mark’s commemorative homily presents Tikhon’s teaching together with his acts of mercy. It connects the saint’s memory with the experience of St.Tikhon’s Monastery and its patronal celebration. This homiletic reception is distinct from the chronological biography.

[3] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 4; Published biographical account,paragraph 14; Published biographical account,paragraph 19

Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

Related Scripture; not a claim that this passage narrates the saint’s life or is a prescribed feast-day reading.

[4] Public-domain Bible translation · Matthew 11: 28–30

Sapaeva portrays visits made in the dress of an ordinary monk and help offered without public display. Her account also names a house used to shelter the sick and the continuing correspondence of his final years.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Published biographical account,paragraph 6; Published biographical account,paragraph 13
